messages.subject: Modeling parasite intensity partially dependent upon distance sampling
messages.subject_clean: Modeling parasite intensity partially dependent upon distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Thank you all for developing such a great tool, I have been having fun learning how to use it!

I am looking to model the following system in INLA / inlabru. The model is for parasite abundance, which is the product of its intensity (in the epidemiological sense, hereafter 'per-sample abundance'), and white-tailed deer scat density. I am seeking this product because it represents a measure of infection risk of the parasites to an aberrant host, the moose.

I want to model the two likelihoods jointly, specifying that per-sample parasite abundance is potentially dependent upon deer scat density (an estimated parameter, proportional to white-tailed deer abundance). However, I'm not entirely sure how to specify this jointly in the syntax of INLA / inlabru, whereas I can perform the models independently. I appreciate any help tremendously!

Parasite abundance

Parasite per-sample abundance model

Deer scat distance sampling model (inlabru version, abridged)

Where
 is the estimated true parasite abundance, a measure of relative infection risk to moose
 is the observed intensity (#parasites per scat),
 is the estimated true parasite intensity (in the epidemiological sense, parasites observed per scat),
 is the observed scat abundance (distsamp data),

 is the estimated true scat abundance,
 is a half-normal detection function with range parameter ,
 are mean-0 Gaussian random fields
 is scat location in space

 the regression coefficients on spatially-referenced covariates

Yes certainly! Thanks so much for taking a look.

The deer scat samples were collected along line transects under routine distance sampling protocol along 100m transects. Therefore, I have locations of the scats, and their perpendicular distance from the transect line.

The deer scat samples were analyzed in the laboratory to quantify the number of parasites per sample. We have also additional collections of deer scats made in previous years, but since those were opportunistic collections, those would only be considered in the per-sample abundance model.

Thank you for your help!!!

Best,
Alec

Hi All,

Apologies in advance if this is a simple or repeated question, but I have been wrestling with this for a while and can't seem to figure it out. I have an object of class "inla" that used a Stack from inla.stack() as the data input. I also have several thousand locations with known covariates that occurred in the model that I would like to predict the response to, but I just can't seem to get it to run. What is the best way to get my prediction data into inlabru::predict? should it also be as a stack? Data.frame with the same column names as covariates in the model? Any guidance would be very helpful.

My error is always: Error in `[[<-`(`*tmp*`, ge$f$label, value = smod) : no such index at level 1 but not sure what this means

Thanks for your time,
Brent

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Predict from inla() object using inlabru::predict
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Predict from inla() object using inlabru::predict
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Using inla() estimated objects directly in inlabru::predict() is experimental, in the sense that it is hard to construct the appropriate data input if the model initially used inla.stack().  Are you able to reformulate the estimation as an inlabru::bru() call? Then inlabru would handle all the inla.stack() calls internally. (You may also need the backend-clean branch of inlabru instead of the CRAN released version)

Using inlabru::generate() (without a formula; this just gives samples from the latent model components) or inla.posterior.sample() may also be easier. There’s also a new related function in INLA with similar functionality mentioned in recent discussions.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Model selection leading to different conclusions
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Model selection leading to different conclusions
messages.body_plain:
Yes.

Definitively.

Every model comparison criteria has a different definition of "better" or "best".

Personally, I suggest computing several different criteria and only reporting a strong conclusion when they all agree on the result.

PS: If you use marginal likelihoods, make sure you have no intrinsic components, or adjust for them (see e.g. inla.doc("rw2")).

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

thanks for your question! Thats a good one. I don`t think there are real guidelines about when areal data is small enough to be treated as point data. However, in my case, the data I work with is also fairly small with around 1000 inhabitants per polygon. This would lead to issues of confidentiality when displaying regional, individual-level regression coefficients at that scale. That`s why I was wondering whether it might be a good idea to treat the polygons as points and create a continuous coefficient surface, which does not highlight "this particular tiny little area" where an unfavorable association between individual risk factors and individual outcome exists. Of course, I could create the smoothed surface after the analysis of the polygon data, but it would have been interesting to compare both approaches.

Best, Boris
>

If I use scale.model=TRUE on a random walk 2, is it correct to say that the precision that is outputted isn't scaled? (ie the option just effects the choice of prior?)

If so, how do I get the posterior of the precision of the scaled component out?

(This question bought to you by a standard deviation parameter [transformed from the quantiles of the precision] of O(30) but a RW2 that deviates from zero of O(1)).

Thanks!

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the scale.model=TRUE implementation is done slightly different than in
the 'scaling intrinsic' paper. Instead of scaling the prior, the model
itself it scaled so to have marginal variance about 1, when precision =
1. If you got some weird results, its likely some other reason for it.

H

messages.subject: Interpreting hotspots in a shared spatial field from a joint model with two species
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting hotspots in a shared spatial field from a joint model with two species
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

We are using a joint model with a shared spatial field to determine the common spatial trends for two different species based on work put forward in Sadykova et al. (2017) - https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.3081.  In the paper, they create a joint model that has a shared spatial field for pairs of different species (using the copy function) in order to identify areas of common spatial trends.  The full code for the joint spatial model is available from the authors here under "Joint Spatial Models":

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1002%2Fece3.3081&file=ece33081-sup-0002-AppendixS2.txt

The shared spatial field part of the model formula and INLA call are below designating a shared spatial field for 3 different species using the copy function (we are only using two species in our case):

  f(i.spat1, model="bym", graph = "graph2.dat", hyper= param.spat01) +
  f(i.spat2, copy="i.spat1", fixed=F) +
  f(i.spat3, copy="i.spat1", fixed=F)

  result.j1 <- inla(formula,family=c("gamma","gamma","gamma"), data=data,
               control.compute=list(dic=T),
               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE), verbose=TRUE,
               control.fixed = list(expand.factor.strategy = "inla"))

Several environmental covariates are also included in the model formula to account for habitat preferences. The resulting spatial field is then plotted to identify hotspots, described in the paper as "residual spatial autocorrelation unexplained by covariates" (Figure 3 from the paper below, pairs of different species assumed to be competitors):

We have been able to plot similar figures for the spatial field (after including covariates as well) and have found analogous hot spots. However, I was just hoping for some ideas on exactly how these spatial dependencies could be interpreted.
Sadykova et al. (2017) in section 4.2.3 of their paper describe hot spot areas as "high activity areas of the coupled species".  However, I am assuming that shared spatial dependence (after taking environmental covariates into account) could also be in areas where there is low "activity" in terms of the absolute numbers of each species?  That is, hotspots on the spatial field would not necessarily correlate with areas where there is the highest number of either species.
Do these hotspots tell us anything about the interaction between these two species at these locations?

In the case of a spatial field for a single response variable, Zuur et al. 2017 (Spatial, Temporal and Spatial-Temporal Ecological Data Analysis with R-INLA) describe an example of bird nests:

“A value of µi = 0.8 at a nest in one of these hotspots has an expected number of fledged chicks that are around exp(0.8) = 2 larger than at a nest not in such a hotspot.” – page 318

Is there a way to characterize a shared spatial field in a similar manner?  Could the posterior means of a shared spatial field also be described in this type of quantitative way when the field represents the shared spatial dependence between both of the species?

Many thanks for the help!

Paul

messages.subject: SPDE across time with missing observations
messages.subject_clean: SPDE across time with missing observations
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I have been trying to create a SPDE model for some snow data, the problem I am running across is that when i make my mesh for all the locations that the snow is being sampled at there are dates that are missing from locations, for example if i had a sample for every date at each location id have 25,000 observations but I have a bit over 17,000. Is there a way to make a model that can go across all time and use all the data i have. Anybody know how to handle this?

Thanks
Clinton Woods

Some basic code:

c <- cbind(xy$lon, xy$lat)

bound <- inla.nonconvex.hull(points = c,
                             convex = 0.2,
                             concave = 0.2)

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(c, boundary = bound,
                     max.edge = c(0.3,0.8),
                     cutoff = 0.1)

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

# hard to make an indicator because each measurement site might have different numbers of observations threw time.
SS$time <- rep(?, each = 115)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh,
                      loc = c,
                      group = SS$Y,
                      n.group = 287)

The code looks fine as it is.(provided that SS only contains the observed values, and not the missing observations)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
This would be the model, like

	y ~ Poisson(eta)

where eta is the linear predictor, but eta>0. does not match well with
being Gaussian. it only make sense if eta is >> 0.
you can add the identity link, but it is on your own risk. I would add
an offset to make it start from something positive.

you can add the identity link, using this 'hack'

> library(INLA)

[7] "special2"

messages.body_plain:
INLA : version 18.07.12
R version 3.4.3  on win7 (64bit)

May I ask a simple question about variant=1 in the family weibull.surv? I've run the same no-random-effects survival model using both survreg (package Survival) and inla. It looks to me as if the result for inla has the signs reversed (for the means) from what I get with survreg (for the estimated coefficients).  (Moreover, the survreg signs are intuitively correct, while those of inla aren't).

Is this expected, possibly a function of the parametrization? I've been staring at the definition of weibull/variant=1 and don't see it.  Also, if it is expected, is there any way to get inla to report the opposite signs (other than, I presume, using negatived covariates in the formula)?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Inverse of projection matrix A (inla.spde.make.A)
messages.subject_clean: Inverse of projection matrix A (inla.spde.make.A)
messages.body_plain:
Values between nodes can be obtained using the projection
matrix A (calculated from inla.mesh.make.A), e.g.,

A_fs = inla.spde.make.A(mesh_s, lonlat_f)
x_f = A_fs%*%x_s

A_sf = inla.spde.make.A(mesh_f, lonlat_s)
x_s = A_sf%*%x_f

My question is whether A_sf can be easily obtained from A_fs.
This is useful in situations where it is not possible to obtain
A_sf as above due to too many f locations.

A naive way to solve this is by using a loop, however this seems
far from optimal, e.g.,

for (int f=0; f<nf; f++) {
    A_1s = A_fs.row(f);
    x_s += A_1s*x_f(f);
}

Any help is appreciated.

Thanks

Chris

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Inverse of projection matrix A (inla.spde.make.A)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
How many points are we talking about here?
The most efficient loop solution would likely be to project on the order of 10^4 to 10^5 points in each iteration.

Preallocate xs
For each subset, do
  Asf <- inla.spde.make.A(meshf, points[subset,])
  xs[subset] <- Asf %*% xf

Are all the points unique or are there duplicates? For duplicate points, it’s more efficient to give only the unique set as “loc” and specify the “index” information that gives  uniqueloc[index,] == originalloc .

But I don’t understand what you intend/mean by inverse projection here. Are you mapping between two meshes? Pointwise evaluation at the nodes will not give a true inverse mapping in that case.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
you have to do like this, where you have to input an positive initial
value for the predictor, the first 'n' elements of 'x', and the rest of
that one, just fill with zero's.

if you have 'theta's you need to add those as well.

it will not like y=0's....

library(INLA)
r=inla.models()
ls(envir=INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())
m = get("inla.models", envir=INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())
m$likelihood$poisson$link = c(m$likelihood$poisson$link, "identity")
assign("inla.models", m, envir = INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())

n = 100

x = rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

lambda = 50 + x

y = rpois(n, lambda = lambda)

y[y==0] = 1
r = inla(y ~ 1 + x,
         family = "poisson",
         control.mode = list(theta = numeric(), x = c(rep(100, n), 0,
0), restart=TRUE),
         data = data.frame(y, x),

         control.family = list(control.link = list(model =
"identity")))

summary(r)

messages.body_plain:
What I am asking is whether there is an efficient way to do the reverse of what
the following is doing,

x_f = A_fs%*%x_s

i.e., is it possible to calculate A_fs^(-1), so the following can be carried out

A_fs^(-1) * x_f = A_fs^(-1) * A_fs * x_s
x_s = A_fs^(-1) * x_f

I have a spde model that uses mesh_s with ns nodes. I am then simulating
fine scale data from this model. The simulated data is on a grid with nf nodes.
It is then desired to project back to the ns nodes.

In my current situation ns is approx 1,000 and nf is approx 300,000. With your
inbuilt inla.spde.make.A function it is trivial to go from ns to nf (i.e., project to the
nf grid from the mesh_s nodes), However, it is not so easy to project in the opposite
direction, particularly when nf = large?

In the said situation there is no mesh_f, this was a red hearing and may be
confusing matters. Note, each nf point is unique.

As there is no mesh_f your above loop is not possible. So far the only solution I
have come up with is the previously described loop, e.g.,

x_s = matrix(0, ncol = ns)
for each grid node f, do
    x_s += A_fs[f, ] * x_f[f]

Is it possible to speed this up in some way (ideally by avoiding loops).

Thank you for your quick response.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Ok, that’s a more clear question!
Since A is rectangular it doesn’t have an inverse, so it’s not a well posed problem; one has to make a choice of which pseudo-inverse is desired.

The least squares solution is an option, easiest obtained via Cholesky factorization of A’A. However, unless the function on the larger set is extremely well behaved, this can easily introduce spurious artifacts.

If the larger set of points is relatively dense in the mesh (and it sounds like that’s your situation) then I’ve had success with a more robust as well as cheaper approach. I’ll see if I can find my example code for that (used for subsampling global high resolution elevation data onto a global lower resolution mesh), or I’ll recreate it.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Inverse of projection matrix A (inla.spde.make.A)
messages.body_plain:
On second thought, it’s faster to just recreate the code...

Let x be the function on the mesh nodes, and let z be the high resolution evaluation, given by (change of notation for ease of email writing):

z = A x

Then

cs <- colSums(A)
xbackprojected <- (t(A) %*% z) / (cs + (cs == 0))
xbackprojected[cs == 0] <- NA

is an approximate inversion.  The ==0 is there to make all-zero columns of A not produce division by zero.  For real world dense data with some this is a simple approach, when one doesn’t want to got to the length of solving the full GMRF inversion just to project dense evaluations onto the mesh. For full noise control, the full GMRF solution is better.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpretation of shared spatial field
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Interpretation of shared spatial field
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

"I am assuming that spatial dependence could also be in areas where there is low "activity" in terms of the absolute numbers of each species, but high spatial dependence?  That is, hot spots on the spatial field would not neccessarily correlate with areas where there is the highest number of either species. "
If I understand hotspot correctly, it is where the spatial field takes large positive values. There you find large activity. If the activity is small, in a spatially dependent way, this will be picked up by the spatial field as large negative values.

To interpret the spatial field it might be easier to think of it as a covariate, a beta*x. In some sense, the spatial field is just a fancy high-dimensional/nonparametric beta*x. You interpret the spatial field in much the same way as a shared covariate effect.
Haakon

messages.subject: How to define a latent model component for hyper parameter using control.family?
messages.subject_clean: How to define a latent model component for hyper parameter using control.family?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am new to INLA. I am trying to build a hierarchical model:

x_i  ~ BetaBinomial(n, eta_i, K_i), eta_i is mean parameter, K is precision parameter

Where  logit(eta_i) = Beta_0+Beta*R_i, R_i is a vector of covariates

We assume:

Beta_0 ~ N(mu, sigma)

Beta ~ MVN(mu_beta, B)

K = (K_1, K_2,…., K_N) ~ MVN( (K_0,….,K_0), tau*D)

K_0 ~ N(mu_k, sigma_k)

tau ~ Inverse-Gamma(a, b)

My question is how can I define the prior for K using INLA function. From what I understand,  control.family can be used to add prior on hyper-parameter K, but it seems I can not define my own precision matrix D^(-1). And also, I don’t know how to add prior to K_0 and tau either.

Thanks so much if you can have a look at my problem and give me some suggestions!

messages.subject: Back-transformation for prediction with inlabru and differences from inla code results
messages.subject_clean: Back-transformation for prediction with inlabru and differences from inla code results
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I trained a model with INLA and I would like now to switch to inlabru to separate the training and the prediction phase. However, I am having difficulties at understanding how to specify the back-transformation for the prediction phase.

Here is my inlabru code:

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Stochastic partial differential equation SPDE model
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## MODEL FIT
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ff <- as.formula(paste(response_var, paste(c('0',predictors, 'mySPDE(map = coordinates, model = spde)'), collapse=" + "),sep='~'))
mod_INLAbru <- bru(ff, data = train, family = "nbinomial", options = list(verbose=TRUE))

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## PREDICTION
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ff <- as.formula(paste(response_var, paste0("exp(",paste(c('0', predictors, 'mySPDE'), collapse=" + "),")"),sep='~'))
INLAbru_predictions <- predict(mod_INLAbru, data = test, formula = ff)

Moreover, when I use INLA - where I can specify the link in the inla call (control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_join), link = 1, compute = TRUE)) - I get different (better, according to the pseudo r2) results (see attached plots). Here is the INLA code:

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## PROJECTOR MATRIX
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A_train <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coords_train)
A_test <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coords_test)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## STACK
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field", n.spde = spde$n.spde)

stack_train <- inla.stack(
 tag = 'train', ## tag
 data = list(response_var = train[[response_var]]), ## response
 A = list(A_train, 1), ## two projector matrices (SPDE and fixed effects)
 effects = list(
 c(
 s.index,
 list(intercept = 1) ## SPATIAL EFFECTS
    ),
 train %>%
 select(predictors) %>% ## FIXED EFFECTS
 as.list()
 )
)

stack_latent <- inla.stack(
 tag = 'latent', ## tag
 data = list(X = NA), ## response
 A = list(A_test), # one projector matrices (SPDE)
 effects = list(s.index) ## SPATIAL EFFECT
)

stack_test <- inla.stack(
 tag = 'test', ## tag
 data = list(response_var = test[[response_var]]), ## response
 A = list(A_test, 1), ## two projector matrices (SPDE and fixed effects)
 effects = list(
 c(
 s.index,
 list(intercept = 1) ## SPATIAL EFFECTS
    ),
 test %>%
 select(predictors) %>% ## FIXED EFFECTS
 as.list()
 )
)

stack_join <- inla.stack(stack_train,stack_latent,stack_test)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## MODEL FIT
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
inla.setOption("num.threads", 2)

ff <- as.formula(paste('response_var', paste(c('0',predictors, 'f(spatial.field, model = spde)'), collapse=" + "),sep='~'))
mod_INLA_start <- inla(
 ff,
 data = inla.stack.data(stack_join, spde=spde),
 family = "nbinomial",
 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_join), link = 1, compute = TRUE),  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
 control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb")
)

mod_INLA <- inla(
 ff,
 data = inla.stack.data(stack_join, spde=spde),
 family = "nbinomial",
 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_join), link = 1, compute = TRUE),  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
 control.mode = list(result = mod_INLA_start, restart = TRUE), verbose = TRUE
)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## PREDICTION
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

index_latent <- inla.stack.index(stack_join, tag = "latent")$data
index_test <- inla.stack.index(stack_join, tag = "test")$data

INLA_predictions_latent <- mod_INLA$summary.fitted.values[index_latent, 1:5]
INLA_predictions <- mod_INLA$summary.fitted.values[index_test, 1:5]

More questions:
- in inlabru is the spde added as a constant term for prediction?
- if I wanted to predict the latent field only, would this be correct?

ff <- as.formula(paste(response_var, paste0("exp(mySPDE)"),sep='~'))
INLAbru_predictions_latent <- predict(mod_INLAbru, data = test, formula = ff)

Many many thanks,

Giulia

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Back-transformation for prediction with inlabru and differences from inla code results
messages.body_plain:
Quick partial response:

the inlabru predictions are based on Monte Carlo estimates via inla.posterior.sample; you probably want to increase the number of samples to reduce the Monte Carlo error, which should may affect the inla/inlabru comparison with respect to the link function.

I’m not sure what you mean wrt the spde as a constant?

The exp(spde) prediction code looks ok. Though the predict() function will ignore the “response variable”, as it’s not needed to define the prediction.

Finn

Bests regards!
Abdoulaye

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to define a latent model component for hyper parameter using control.family?
messages.body_plain:
Amelia,

We usually don't do models like this in INLA where the likelihood has two parameters indexed by "i". This does not mean that it is impossible, but I believe it is not implemented.

We are working on a paper dealing with this class of models, with Birgir Hrafnkelsson, I can let you know when we have a first Arxiv version. However, this approach assumes you have more than 1 observation per index i.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatio-temporal hurdle model prediction
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatio-temporal hurdle model prediction
messages.body_plain:
¡SOLVED!

I am trying to adjust a spatio-temporal shared hurdle model (binomial, gamma) for fisheries data where the sampling points are spatially different over the years.

I have 2 datasets. The observation dataset (data) has the columns for presence/absence , counts and environmental variables at the different sampling locations over the years (4 years). The prediction dataset (cov) has the environmental variable values extracted at the mesh points (1675 points), repeated 1 time for each one of the 4 years (so length(cov$lat)=6700 points).

Both datasets have an index column "year" indicating 1 repeated as many times as points in the first year, 2 for the second year...etc.

I have done the prediction just for 1 year  without any problem because length (cov$year==1) = length (mesh.points).

However, I am getting this error when I try to predict in all years because length (cov$year )!= length (mesh.points).

#error code ---------------------------------------------------------------

est.temp <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=matrix(c(data$Long,data$Lat),ncol=2),
                             group=data$Year,
                             n.group=max(data$Year))

pred.temp <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
                              group=max(unique(data$Year)),
                              n.group=length(unique(data$Year)))

Error in (function (data, A, effects, tag = "", compress = TRUE, remove.unused = TRUE)  :
  Row count mismatch for A: 1675,6696

* I have also tried to indicate in est.pred group=cov$year and n.group=length(unique(cov$year)) as I saw in another example from this group but it`s not the correct way.

SOLUTION:

The "inla.spde.make.A" call needs to be told about what locations to use. By default, loc=mesh$loc, so if you want to predict for different years, you should indicate the repeated locations for each year with the index parameter: index=rep(1:mesh$n, times=number of years)

And the same occurs for the structure within the group parameter: group=rep(sort(unique(data$Year)),each=mesh$n)

Fran.

n_{t-1}; with n ~ N(0,tau_n)
where we estimate tau, which should have a largely uninformative prior. The same goes for e of course.

f(t, X, model = "rw1", values = seq(1,3,1)).

But I am not sure if this is actually a valid solution or if I get into different issues then.

messages.subject: Overfitting on a Gamma regression model
messages.subject_clean: Overfitting on a Gamma regression model
messages.body_plain:
I trying to fit a complex mixed-effects model using INLA.

The model family is specified as "Gamma".

However, it appears as if I'm experiencing significant overfitting.

For my work process, I am using 10% of the data as a hold-out test set.  This is done by setting the dependent value to NA for those rows.

The errors for the hold-out data rows are much larger than the erros for the rows will full data.

As a diagnostic step, I fit a much simpler model with just an intercept and one very clear random effect (group)

The marginal mean for the both the intercept and the single RE seem very reasonable and closely match both domain expertise and empirical summary of the data.

For this simple, model, the fit is still significantly better for the training rows than the testing rows.

Something surprising are the actual predicted values.  For the test data (with dependent variable set to NA), the marginal mean of the predicted values are the sum of the intercept and the matching random effect. (as expected).  Rows within the same group (random effect) have the exact same predicted mean value.  Intuitively, this makes sense, as the model has no other information except for intercept and the one random effect.

HOWEVER, for the training data, the marginal mean of the predicted values are different - rows within the same group vary quite a bit (unlike the test rows) and their predicted values are much closer to the actual ground truth.

The net result is that the error for the training rows is very very small, and the error for the test rows is very very high.  Since the model ONLY has intercept and a single random effect, how is this possible?

Additionally, would tuning the prior for the Gamma family model help resolve this?  If so, how/where can I do that?

Thanks a million!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Since the predictor includes all the latent components, such as the random effect, it should be much closer to the observed data. But that depends on the details of the random effect structure; Perhaps the principle you use for comparing the fit is based on not including the random effect in the predicted values for the data used in estimation, but you’re using the full predictions from InLa, that does include them?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
First of all, E(exp(x)) is not equal to exp(E(x)), so you’re not actually assessing the posterior mean of (x) when you exponentiate the posterior mean of x.
Set control.predictor=list(link=1) and use summary.fitted.values instead to make inla provide E(exp(x)) directly.
Since the posterior mean of exo(x) also involves the posterior variance of x, the results can differ dramatically.

That the linear predictor values are different within each group in the training data may or may not be a “real thing”; are they just numerically different but practically equal? (i.e small in comparison to the posterior standard deviations) That’s what one should expect from the way the numerics are done.
If not, perhaps you have a badly scaled model?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear users,

I did a simulation study in 2017 using the SPDE model with INLA and I was very happy to have very good results. Now, I can not run the same models that worked very well just a year ago, what has changed in INLA () function ?

My model :

ModelSPDE.INLA <- inla(formula, family="weibullsurv", data=inla.stack.data(stk), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk)),
                       control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,mlik=TRUE),control.inla = list (strategy = "laplace"),verbose=TRUE)

See below the error message production by my model :

GMRFLib version 3.0-0-snapshot, has recived error no [12]
Reason    : The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message   : Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
Function  : GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern
File      : approx-inference.c
Line      : 2936
RCSId     : file: approx-inference.c  hgid: b52758cff626  date: Mon Sep 24 12:43:35 2018 +0300

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

Bests regards
Guindo

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2019-02-26 at 02:38 -0800, syaroni...@gmail.com wrote:
> 1. The credibility intervals containing zero, does it means that the
> covariates are not significant effecting the respon.?

Would be nice if that was true in general ;-)  Marginally it is similar
to this, but it gives an indication at least.

> 2.  I measure the Fraction Spatial and the results is 0.992. When the
> iid component is very high and the spatial component is low, as I
> know the Fraction spatial is the ratio between structure spatial
> effect and all spatial effect. Is my results correct or not.?

I see where you're heading, but the answer is no. there is a 'correct' bym model,
implemented in 'bym2' (see this paper for the refernence https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01180)
and you'll find it print yourself. the paper will answer why this is not correct, and
also how to fix it. see also inla.doc("bym2")

H

messages.subject_clean: R-INLA crashing
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running a spatial-temporal Bernoulli model on aquatic plant presence/absence data (response) and a number of explanatory variables. However, INLA keeps crashing. I have tried many different meshes and have also added scale=T and hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec",param=c(1,0.01))) as was recommended on this forum in the past. However, no luck so far.

Any insights would be much appreciated!

Here is my code and the verbose=T output.

My R code:

datafile.final2$YearSeq <- as.numeric(as.factor(datafile.final2$Year))
NYear <- length(unique(datafile.final2$YearSeq))

mesh2 <- inla.mesh.create.helper(points=cbind(datafile.final2$x, datafile.final2$y),max.edge=c(10000,30000), cutoff=2000)

coords <- as.matrix(datafile.final2[,1:2])

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh2, alpha=2)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh2, loc=coords,group=datafile.final2$YearSeq,n.group = NYear)

time.index <- inla.spde.make.index("w", n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group = NYear)

#standardize explanatory variables

datafile.final2$secchi.std <- (datafile.final2$secchi-mean(datafile.final2$secchi))/sd(datafile.final2$secchi)
datafile.final2$PLW.std <- (datafile.final2$PLW-mean(datafile.final2$PLW))/sd(datafile.final2$PLW)
datafile.final2$Phos.std <- (datafile.final2$Phos-mean(datafile.final2$Phos))/sd(datafile.final2$Phos)
datafile.final2$Nit.std <- (datafile.final2$Nit-mean(datafile.final2$Nit))/sd(datafile.final2$Nit)
datafile.final2$salinity.std <- (datafile.final2$salinity-mean(datafile.final2$salinity))/sd(datafile.final2$salinity)
datafile.final2$neighbors.std <- (datafile.final2$neighbors-mean(datafile.final2$neighbors))/sd(datafile.final2$neighbors)
datafile.final2$total.area.std <- (datafile.final2$total.area-mean(datafile.final2$total.area))/sd(datafile.final2$total.area)
datafile.final2$distance.to.edge.std <- (datafile.final2$distance.to.edge-mean(datafile.final2$distance.to.edge))/sd(datafile.final2$distance.to.edge)
datafile.final2$distance.between.beds.std <- (datafile.final2$distance.between.beds-mean(datafile.final2$distance.between.beds))/sd(datafile.final2$distance.between.beds)

N <- nrow(datafile.final2)

X <- data.frame(Intercept=rep(1,N), datafile.final2$secchi.std,datafile.final2$PLW.std,datafile.final2$Phos.std,datafile.final2$Nit.std,datafile.final2$salinity.std,datafile.final2$neighbors.std, datafile.final2$total.area.std, datafile.final2$distance.to.edge.std,datafile.final2$distance.between.beds.std)

colnames(X) <- c("Intercept","secchi.std","PLW.std","Phos.std","Nit.std","salinity.std","neighbors.std","total.area.std", "distance.to.edge.std","distance.between.beds.std")

stack3 <- inla.stack(data=list(y=datafile.final2$pres, link=1,Ntrials=1),A=list(A,1),effects=list(w=time.index, X=as.data.frame(X)), tag="est")

hyper1 <- list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec",param=c(1,0.01)))

formula3 <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + secchi.std+PLW.std+Phos.std+Nit.std+salinity.std+neighbors.std + total.area.std + distance.to.edge.std+distance.between.beds.std + f(w, model=spde,group=w.group,control.group = list(model="ar1",scale.model = T),hyper=hyper1)

data = inla.stack.data(stack3)

r3 <- inla(formula3, control.inla=list(reordering="metis"),family="binomial",Ntrials=1, data=data, control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T,config=T),control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack3), compute=T, link=1, quantiles=c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),verbose = T)

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I want to fit the following model to a dataset using INLA:

  Y_{i,j}  is  Poisson( mu_{i,j} ),   i = 1, ..., n, j = 1, ..., m,

  log mu_{i,j} = a_{i} + b_{i} c_{j} + v_{j}

  a_{i} and b_{i} are fixed effects
  c_{j} is an AR(1) random effect
  v_{j} is an iid random effect

Is it possible to fit such a model in R-INLA? If so, what would be the correct model formula?

  Y ~ a + b ?? f(j, model="ar1") + f(j, model="iid")

Many thanks in advance.

Best regards,

Abdollah

Hi,
The nonlinear predictor approximation method in the inlabru package can handle this.
See inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> for tutorial examples. There are some quirks in how one needs to define the formula to make the optimizer work, but it’s mostly a matter of defining he model components and then providing an R expression evaluating the desired predictor expression.

Finn

I guess the answer here, is

- upgrade to the most recent testing version
- get a license for pardiso, see inla.pardiso()
- have a server with enough RAM
- use
 control.compute=list(openmp.strategy = "pardiso.parallel")
  or 'pardiso.serial', as described in inla.pardiso()

H

forgot, and add

	inla.setOption(mkl=TRUE)

which enables the build with the Intel-MKL libraries instead of
OpenBLAS.

>

> - have a server with enough RAM
> - use

>   or 'pardiso.serial', as described in inla.pardiso()
